title: The browser no longer overwrites the saved admin login when a password changes
subtitle: Sample page for a synthetic change in a made-up web app (Acme Portal)

conclusions.requests: Both requests you kept are done, one after a second attempt because the first missed a form; the third check was redirected to a local browser and is not counted.
conclusions.map: Only the web front end changed: the admin screen and the sign-in screens. The server stays as it was because it never touched the admin password.
conclusions.logic: Password forms had no username field, so the browser tied the new password to the admin login it had saved. Each form now carries a hidden username field with the right person's email.
conclusions.rationale: A hidden username field fixes what the browser sees; a server fix cannot. The browser's reaction on the create-user form is inferred from how browsers behave and has no test.
conclusions.evidence: The new tests failed before the fix and pass after it, and a real browser showed the right prompt before and after. A second browser version and the deployed build are unchecked.

modules.name: Browser password manager
modules.summary: The user's own browser, where the save and update prompts appear. Outside the code base.

logic.before_title: Before: password forms have no username field
logic.after_title: After: each form names the right person

before.label: Change-password form: passwords only
before.text: The page has three fields: current password, new password, repeat. Nothing says which account the password belongs to.

before.label: The browser picks the saved admin login
before.text: With no username in the form, the browser attaches the new password to the admin login it already saved.

before.label: Sign-out lands on the login page
before.text: After a change, the app ends the session and shows the login page, where the browser offers to update the admin password.

visual.title: Update password?
visual.subtitle: for admin, though another person just changed theirs

after.label: Change password: hidden username
after.text: The form carries a hidden username field with the signed-in person's email, next to the password fields.

after.label: Reset password: hidden username
after.text: The reset form carries the email of the person being reset, not the admin who clicks the button.

after.label: Create user: email is the username
after.text: The email field being typed is already the username of the first password, so no second hidden field is needed.

after.label: The browser offers the right save
after.text: The browser sees a username in the same form as the new password and offers to save it for that person. The saved admin entry stays untouched.

visual.title: Save password?
visual.subtitle: for the person who just changed it

examples.text: Local browser run before the fix: prompt "Update password?" for admin@example.test. After the fix: "Save password?" for member@example.test, the person who changed it.

chosen.text: Fix it in the interface and leave the server alone.

rejected.why_not: The server never changed the admin password; logging in with the original password still worked.

rejected.option: Add a second hidden field on the create-user form
rejected.why_not: The email field already is the username; a hidden copy would need to stay in sync with it.

tradeoff.text: The create-user form has no current-password field, so browsers most likely treat it as a sign-up form. That is an inference about browser behaviour and has no test.

ran.detail: Before the fix both reset-form tests failed. After it, all pass.
